decisions.quote: To address these limitations, in 2022 I designed an online experiment closely following Jahn's (2004, Experiment 1) design and using Jahn's stimulus sentences translated into Bulgarian). Administration was individual and the order of sentences randomized. Unlike Bransford et al. (1972), I found no significant model type (same/different) by probe type (old/new) interaction effect on the recognition scores. Unlike Rinck et al. (2001), the main effect of model type for new sentences was not significant, although it was in the expected direction. Unlike Jahn (2004) there was no significant model type by scene type (predator/peaceful) interaction effect on recognition scores. Due to a bug in the experiment script, some sentence groups occurred more often than others. Now I aim to replicate Bransford et al.'s, Rinck et al.'s, and Jahn's results, with a new improved script and with a new set of participants.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state files exist for this work. This prospective OSF registration closely follows the design and translated stimulus sentences of Jahn (2004, Experiment 1) in a new Bulgarian sample and explicitly retests Jahn's empirical findings: Confirmatory Hypothesis 2 tests the model-type main effect on new sentences (following Rinck et al., 2001 and Jahn, 2004) and Confirmatory Hypothesis 3 tests Jahn's (2004) specific model-type (same/different) by scene-type (predator/peaceful) interaction on new sentences. The reference list (q23) and Crossref metadata establish the original identity as Jahn, G. (2004), 'Three turtles in danger: Spontaneous construction of causally relevant spatial situation models', Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 30(5), 969-987 (10.1037/0278-7393.30.5.969). decisions.location: Results — Partial replication: a chromatin-mediated reversible drug-tolerant state in cancer cell subpopulations; Materials and methods; References
decisions.quote: As part of the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, we published a Registered Report ( Haven et al., 2016 ) that described how we intended to replicate selected experiments from the paper ‘A chromatin-mediated reversible drug-tolerant state in cancer cell subpopulations’ ( Sharma et al., 2010 ). We attempted to independently replicate experiments that tested the phenotype of a small subpopulation of ‘drug-tolerant persister’ cells (DTPs) that are generated when PC9 cells, a protein-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI)-sensitive non-small cell lung cancer cell line, is exposed to high concentrations of TKIs.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication confirmed target_index 0 as an omitted target (while rejecting targets 7-10 as initiated protocols stopped without results). Independently verified: this article reports new experimental replication data, methods, and an OSF dataset (Figure 1A-D, Figure 1-figure supplement 1, https://osf.io/xbign/) retesting Sharma et al. (2010), specifically measuring DTP viability percentages in PC9 cells after 9 days of erlotinib treatment (~6% at 2 uM vs ~0.3% in the original; ~1% at 20 uM), survival IC50 (~0.15 uM vs ~0.0085 uM in the original), and EGFR phosphorylation inhibition (>1 uM vs <0.01 uM in the original) before stopping prior to downstream IGF-1R/KDM5A experiments. Haven et al. (2016) is the replicating team's own Stage 1 Registered Report protocol, whereas the reference list and Crossref metadata identify the retested original study as Sharma et al. (2010), Cell 141:69-80 (10.1016/j.cell.2010.02.027). All five shipped rows (425: Kan et al., 2010; 488: Heidorn et al., 2010; 489: Johannessen et al., 2010; 490: Lu et al., 2012; 491: Ricci-Vitiani et al., 2010) and sibling target_index 5 (Kang et al., 2011) are independent original studies by different authors on different cancer biology mechanisms; report equivalence does not apply.

decisions.quote: As part of the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, we published a Registered Report ( Raouf et al., 2015 ) that described how we intended to replicate selected experiments from the paper ‘Senescence surveillance of pre-malignant hepatocytes limits liver cancer development’ ( Kang et al., 2011 ). Since then a study reported tumor-specific CD8 T cells arose independently of CD4 T cells, but needed Th1-polarized CD4 T cells to effectively suppress tumorigenesis supporting the crucial role CD4 T cells play in tumor suppression by immunosurveillance ( Knocke et al., 2016 ). We attempted to independently replicate experiments that tested the immune clearance of premalignant senescent hepatocytes and the dependence on CD4 + T cells.

decisions.quote: McCann and Bahl is one of the first studies to examine the link between the threat of informal competition and new product development by formal firms in developing economies. Grounding their logic in attention-based view, McCann and Bahl find a positive association between informal competition and development of new products, which is weakened by the presence of formal firms, prevalence of irregular payments, and optimism about the regulatory environment. Our investigation examines the reproducibility of McCann and Bahl with the same data and its replication in a different time-period and across different country sub-samples.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state files exist for this work. Target_index 0 ('McCann; Bahl', 2017) is already represented by shipped row input_row_index 1483 (McCann & Bahl, 'The influence of competition from informal firms on new product development', DOI 10.1002/smj.2585, year_o 2016). The replicating paper is titled 'Does competition from informal firms impact new product development? Systematic replication and extension of McCann and Bahl (2017)' and re-examines McCann and Bahl's exact finding on informal competition and new product development by formal firms in developing economies. Crossref metadata for 10.1002/smj.2585 confirms that Brian T. McCann and Mona Bahl's article 'The influence of competition from informal firms on new product development' was published online on October 26, 2016 (accounting for shipped year_o 2016) and in print in Strategic Management Journal Vol. 38, Issue 7, pp. 1518-1535 in 2017 (accounting for 'McCann and Bahl (2017)' in the replication title). Because the blind coder had only the abstract without the reference list, title and DOI were left empty and the 2016 online vs. 2017 issue year discrepancy prevented automatic matching, but both refer to the exact same original study.

decisions.quote: We were able to replicate the use of several PLR metrics as a biomarker for mTBI diagnosis that could easily be included with standard clinical measures.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state files exist for this work. The supplied primary source is restricted to the title and abstract, which state that the study replicated the use of pupillary light reflex (PLR) metrics as a diagnostic biomarker for mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) in 196 US Military Academy cadets across preinjury baseline, within 48 hours post-mTBI, asymptomatic, and unrestricted return-to-activity time points, but never cite or name the original study or studies being replicated (leaving blind_target authors, year, title, and DOI empty). Shipped row input_row_index 1283 (Dengler et al., 2024, 'Quantitative Pupillometry Predicts Return to Play and Tracks the Clinical Evolution of Mild Traumatic Brain Injury in US Military Academy Cadets: A Military Traumatic Brain Injury Initiative Study', Neurosurgery, 10.1227/neu.0000000000003032) shares seven of the eight authors and the exact cadet pupillometry paradigm and is very plausibly the retested original work, but without the full text or reference list the available primary evidence cannot settle the retested target's bibliographic identity or whether target_index 0 is identical to shipped row 1283 versus an additional omitted study.
